notes:
I could only search part of this passage. A total of 13 searches and fetches were allowed, and the Enduring Word chapter page cut off before reaching v. 25. That means I have no notes on **vv. 26, 27, 30, 33, 35–37 and 43–45**. I also found no Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Orthodox sources, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage. Everything below comes from pages I actually read.

---

**v. 28**
- Sam Storms (charismatic) uses this verse to explain why the sin in v. 31 is against the Spirit: it was by the power of the Spirit that Jesus did his healings and miracles, and Jesus himself said in Matthew 12:28 that he cast out demons "by the Spirit of God." https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/new-insights-into-the-unpardonable-sin-or-blasphemy-of-the-holy-spirit

**v. 29**
- Pulpit Commentary: the meaning is plain. The strong man is Satan, his goods are the people he afflicts, and the one who ties him up is Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/12.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word): Jesus is stronger than the strong man. Guzik also draws a lesson for spiritual warfare: Jesus lets believers use His name and authority, which gives them the strength to bind the strong man. He adds that nothing in a believer's life has to stay under Satan's control. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/

**vv. 31–32: the "unpardonable sin." This is where traditions differ most.**

*What the sin is (the traditional reading)*
- Ellicott: the best manuscripts read "against the Spirit," without the word "Holy." He says the Pharisees were being warned about a sin they were getting dangerously close to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-31.htm
- Benson: the sin is saying that the devil did miracles which Christ had clearly shown He did by the Holy Spirit. (same URL)
- Clarke: it is neither more nor less than crediting the devil with miracles Christ did by God's power. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/matthew/12-31.html
- Clarke also reassures worried readers: no one who believes Jesus was sent by God can ever commit this sin. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/web/matthew/12-31.html
- Bengel separates sinning against the Spirit from blaspheming the Spirit. Meyer says that for a Christian it would mean going to the very limit of falling away from Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-31.htm
- Gill (a Calvinist reading): the promise that "every sin" will be forgiven does not cover everyone. It applies to those God has promised forgiveness to in His covenant of grace, for whom Christ's blood was shed. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/matthew/12-31.html

*"Either in this age or in the one to come" (v. 32)*
- Barnes: the phrase means the guilt will never be pardoned. It does not imply that any sins are forgiven in hell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-31.htm

*Can a Christian commit it? Reformed and Baptist answers*
- The Gospel Coalition essay (Reformed) sets out four views. Most early church fathers took the view that the sin is saying something false about the Spirit. The essay itself follows Calvin's view: the sin cannot be forgiven because God never enables that person to repent and believe, so only unbelievers can commit it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-unpardonable-sin/
- R. C. Sproul (Ligonier) argues that in theory only a Christian could commit it, because only Christians have the Spirit's clear revelation that Jesus is the Son of God. In practice none will, because Jesus intercedes to keep believers from falling. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/what-unpardonable-sin
- Another Ligonier devotional says Jesus does not say the Pharisees had already crossed the line; they were close, and He was warning them. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blasphemy-of-the-spirit
- John Piper (Baptist, Desiring God), following Alford: the sin is a wilful, determined opposition to the Spirit's present power, and Christians cannot commit that kind of sin. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/can-a-christian-blaspheme-the-holy-spirit
- Desiring God article: if you worry about it, you are most likely not there, because hearts hardened against Jesus don't worry about it. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-is-the-unforgivable-sin

*Charismatic and Arminian voices*
- Sam Storms: the sin is not unforgivable because of any defect in Christ's atoning death. It is unforgivable because it puts a person beyond repentance. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/new-insights-into-the-unpardonable-sin-or-blasphemy-of-the-holy-spirit
- On the same page, a reader's comment (not Storms) raises the Arminian objection: if Calvinist unconditional election is true, the whole question is moot. (same URL)
- J. Vernon McGee applies the passage to today: the sin is choosing to refuse the pardon God offers through the Holy Spirit's convicting work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mcgee_j_vernon/eBooks/unpardonable-sin.cfm

**v. 34**
- McGee links this verse to v. 31: what condemns a person is not the words but the attitude of the heart behind them. (McGee URL above)

**vv. 38–39**
- Barnes: the sign of Jonah means the evidence the Ninevites had that Jonah came from God, namely that he had been miraculously preserved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/12-39.html
- Coffman: "adulterous" refers to Israel's rejection of its covenant with God, not just to the people's morals. (same URL)
- Matthew Henry: the sign is Christ's resurrection from the dead by his own power. (same URL)
- Calvin: Christ means that one sign would stand for all, because they did not deserve to have their ungodly demand granted. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom32/calcom32.ii.xvii.html
- Geneva Study Bible: "adulterous" means a bastard generation that fell away from Abraham's faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-39.htm

**v. 40: the "three days and three nights" problem**
- Bengel: Jesus was in the earth three days but only two nights. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-40.htm
- Meyer: following the common way of counting, parts of the first and third days count as whole days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-40.htm
- Gill: the phrase means three natural days of twenty-four hours each. Barnes: "heart of the earth" means the grave. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/matthew/12-40.html
- Modern scholarship:
  - Barclay notes that Luke's version does not mention the fish at all. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/12-29.html
  - He holds that this verse is Matthew's explanation, not Jesus' own words. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/12-40.html
  - Meyer reports critics who see v. 40 as an "awkward interpolation." Ellicott replies that Jonah's preaching was not a "sign" in any sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/12-40.htm

**vv. 41–42**
- Guzik, quoting Barclay: Jesus is effectively saying "I am God's sign." The Ninevites recognized God's warning in Jonah, and the Queen of Sheba recognized God's wisdom in Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-12/
- Barclay: Jesus claims to be greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon, the height of wisdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/12-29.html

**vv. 46–50: Jesus' "brothers." Protestants and Catholics differ here.**
- Pulpit outline: this section shows opposition to Jesus from his own relatives (vv. 46–50), following opposition from his enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/12.htm
- NET Bible note (modern scholarship): Epiphanius taught that Mary had no children besides Jesus, and others said the brothers were cousins. Nothing in the text suggests any of this. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mat+12%3A46-50
- Protestant views:
  - GotQuestions says the most natural reading is that Jesus had real half-siblings by blood. It adds that Greek had a word for "cousin," and it was not used. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-siblings.html
  - Guzik quotes Clarke: Jesus was Mary's first-born, but no one can prove he was her last. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/
- Catholic views:
  - Jerome, writing against Helvidius, argued that the brothers of the Lord were his cousins, not his own brothers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3007.htm
  - Catholic Answers offers two possibilities: the brothers could be Joseph's sons, but not Mary's, or cousins, since Aramaic had no word for "cousin." It also asks why Jesus would entrust Mary to John at the cross if she had other sons. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/was-mary-a-perpetual-virgin
  - Citing the Catechism, Catholic Answers points out that James and Joseph are sons of another Mary, whom Matthew calls "the other Mary." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-case-for-marys-perpetual-virginity
- Don Stewart (Blue Letter Bible) notes that the stepbrothers view was held by Epiphanius and Jerome, and in modern times by Lightfoot. https://www.blueletterbible.org/faq/don_stewart/don_stewart_199.cfm
  - Note: this attributes the stepbrothers view to Jerome, but Jerome's own tract argues for cousins (see above). The two sources disagree.
